Right, so the real difference between ceramic and porcelain in a wet bathroom comes down to density and water absorption. Porcelain is fired hotter and longer, making it much denser. When we talk about "impervious" in tile terms, we mean it absorbs less than 0.5% water by weight. That's the key metric here.

In a shower environment, that 0.5% makes a huge difference. Ceramic tiles absorb more water—usually between 3-7%—which means they can actually soak up moisture over time. This isn't the tile itself failing, but the water can migrate through the body of the tile.

The installation process is similar, but porcelain requires a better substrate. It's less forgiving of uneven surfaces because it's thicker and stiffer. Ceramic is a bit more flexible, which can actually be an advantage on older homes with slightly wavy subfloors.

Cost-wise, you're looking at about 15-20% more for porcelain, but that's mainly for the better quality control. The basic installation labor is the same. If you're going to redo the floor anyway, the extra upfront cost for porcelain usually pays off in durability.

The one exception where ceramic might make sense is if you're doing a very specific decorative pattern that's only available in ceramic. But for a standard shower floor, porcelain's absorption rate makes it the safer choice.

Underfloor heating isn’t just bolting a mat down and calling it done. You’ve got to prep the subfloor so the system doesn’t cook itself or crack your tiles. Here’s the real deal:

First, your subfloor has to be flat within 1/8” over a 10-foot span. Any deeper dips and you’re sanding for hours or mixing more self-leveler than you want to think about.

If your floor is concrete, you can lay a heating mat directly on it, but you still need a thin layer of bonding agent so the tile adhesive sticks. If it’s plywood, you’ll want to upgrade to exterior-grade (like 3/4” T&G) and screw it down tight—otherwise, the heat will make the joints flex and your tiles will ring like cheap bells.

The heating mat itself is usually electric—thin, flexible, and rated for tile floors. You run a thermostat to control it, and the whole thing sits under your tile layer.

You’ll also need a backer board rated for heat. Regular cement board works, but some brands, like Ditra, have integrated decoupling layers that handle thermal expansion better. They cost more, but they save you from cracked grout lines when the floor bakes and cools.

Speaking of expansion, you’ll want to leave a 1/4” gap around the room’s perimeter so the floor can move without buckling.

One more thing: your electrician needs to run a dedicated circuit. A 15-amp line might handle a small bathroom, but if you’re covering more than 50 square feet, you’ll want 20 amps or you’ll trip the breaker every time you turn on the shower and the heat at the same time.

And whatever you do, do NOT install a hydronic (water-based) system in an upstairs bathroom. Those need a boiler, pumps, and extra insulation. It’s overkill, costs more than the tile budget, and if a pipe leaks, you’re gutting the whole floor. Stick with electric—it’s simpler, cheaper, and you can DIY it without a plumber.

So, prep the subfloor, choose your mat, install a backer board that respects heat, leave room for expansion, and hire a sparky to wire it up. Once that’s done, tiling is just another layer of the same process.

You want to be smart about subfloor prep if you're thinking about adding underfloor heating later. You don't want to rip up the whole bathroom in a year just because you forgot a step now.

First, your subfloor needs to be flat within a quarter-inch over a ten-foot span. If it's not, the heating cables or mats will bridge gaps and burn out. Use a straightedge to check. If you've got dips, pour self-leveling compound. Don't skimp on it; you'll regret it when the tiles crack.

Second, moisture barrier. You're in a bathroom, and water loves to migrate. If your subfloor is plywood, you need a vapor barrier like sheet plastic under the underlayment. Brands like Ditra or Schluter work. They also help with water drainage if you're doing a shower pan, but even for a floor, the decoupling is worth it.

Fourth, spacing for the heating elements. If you're using cable, you need to plan the spacing so you're not overheating any spot. Usually, you want the cables spaced so the floor temperature stays below 85°F at the surface. You'll need a thermostat with a floor sensor to keep it from cooking your feet.

Fifth, electrical. You need a dedicated circuit for the heating. If you're running cable, you'll need to drill through the subfloor to chase the wires to the disconnect box. Do this now, not after you've laid tile.

Finally, leave a chase for the thermostat wiring. If you don't, you'll be cutting into tile later. Run the wires in a PVC conduit under the floor and bring them up through a hole in the tile.

Got it—let’s keep this tight and useful. For underfloor heating in a bathroom, you need three things: a solid base, a conductive screed, and proper isolation. Here’s the short version:

1. **Subfloor must be solid and level** – Any flex will telegraph through the screed and crack your tiles. If your existing subfloor is plywood, add a layer of cement board (12 mm AquaBoard or equivalent) screwed to the joists. Use a self-levelling compound to bring it within 2 mm over 2 m.

2. **Isolation layer** – Lay a 3 mm XPS foam sheet over the board. This keeps heat moving up, not sideways into the joists, and stops thermal bridging. Ribbed foam is fine; flat is cheaper and works too.

3. **Concrete screed** – You’ll need a minimum 50 mm sand-cement screed (1:4 mix) to encase the heating cables or mats. Add fibre mesh to prevent shrinkage cracks. Wait 28 days for full cure before tiling.

4. **Expansion joints** – Cut the screed every 3 m and around the perimeter. Tile over the joints with flexible mastic; don’t grout across them.

5. **Cable spacing** – Stick to the manufacturer’s max spacing (usually 150 mm) to avoid hot spots and keep the floor under 28 °C surface temp.

6. **Damp-proof membrane** – If your bathroom isn’t already tanked, roll a 1.5 mm SBR sheet over the screed before tiling. Lap edges 150 mm and seal with compatible tape.

7. **Thermostat** – Install a floor sensor plus room stat. Set floor max to 28 °C; anything hotter risks grout fatigue and blistered tiles.

If your current subfloor is already a solid concrete slab, skip step 1 and just add the foam, screed, and membrane. For joisted floors, skip step 2 and go straight to board then screed.

Bottom line: level base, foam isolation, 50 mm screed, expansion joints, and a floor sensor. Do that and your tiles will stay put for decades.

**Ceramic vs. Porcelain in a Wet Bathroom**

The difference comes down to how the clay is made and how much water it soaks up.

**Ceramic**
- Clay body is softer, fired at a lower temperature (about 1800°F).
- **Water absorption:** 0.5–3%. That’s porous.
- In a bathroom, moisture can seep through the tile body, through the grout, and into your subfloor. You need a waterproof membrane under it or you risk mold.
- The glaze on top is the only thing keeping water off the surface. If the glaze chips, water gets in.

**Porcelain**
- Clay is denser, fired hotter (2200°F+), often under pressure.
- **Water absorption:** Under 0.5%. Technically, anything under 0.5% is classified as porcelain.
- Water can’t get through the tile itself. It’s essentially waterproof.
- Less likely to crack from freeze-thaw if you ever have a cold basement bathroom.

**What this means for your guest bath:**
- **Ceramic:** Fine for walls, but risky for floors unless you have perfect waterproofing underneath. Cheaper, but you’re paying for the membrane labor.
- **Porcelain:** Safe for floors, walls, even shower pans. More expensive tile, but you save on waterproofing worries.

**Quick test:**
Flip a tile over. If the body is white and uniform, it’s porcelain. If it’s reddish or speckled clay, it’s ceramic.

**Bottom line:**
If you want zero headaches with water, go porcelain. If you’re on a budget and willing to do proper prep, ceramic works. But don’t skimp on the membrane either way.

Underfloor heating adds a layer of complexity to grout selection because you’re dealing with constant thermal cycling—basically, the tile expands and contracts every time the heat cycles on and off. Here’s what you need to know to keep your renovation looking pristine for years:

**1. Choose an epoxy or urethane grout**  
- Cement-based grout shrinks and cracks when heated, so skip it for heated floors.  
- Epoxy grout is virtually indestructible: zero water absorption, no shrinkage, and it won’t yellow.  
- Urethane grout is more flexible, so it handles the thermal movement better than epoxy and is easier to work with.  

**2. Color matters more than you think**  
- Lighter grout hides the inevitable dust and soap scum but shows mold.  
- Darker grout masks mold but highlights dust and chalky residue.  
- For a spa-like look, match the grout to the tile; for a high-contrast look, go two shades darker for definition.  

**3. Sealing: skip it for epoxy, maintain it for urethane**  
- Epoxy grout is non-porous and never needs sealing.  
- Urethane grout is low-porous but can benefit from a light sealant once a year to keep it looking fresh.  

**4. Thermal expansion joints**  
- Your installer should leave a 1/4-inch gap at the edges of the room.  
- Fill it with a flexible silicone caulk, not grout, to allow the tile to expand without cracking.  

**5. Cleaning routine**  
- Avoid acidic cleaners; they can etch the surface of both grout and tile.  
- A mild pH-balanced soap and a soft mop are all you need for routine cleaning.  

**6. Warranty considerations**  
- Check the manufacturer’s warranty; most epoxy grouts come with a lifetime warranty against cracking and staining.  
- Urethane grouts typically have a 10-year warranty, which is still better than cement-based grout.  

**Bottom line:**  
For underfloor heating, urethane grout is the sweet spot—flexible, durable, and affordable. Epoxy is the gold standard if budget isn’t a concern.

Porcelain is harder, more durable, and about twice as expensive per square foot.

**Comparative breakdown**

| Property | Ceramic Tile | Porcelain Tile |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | Common clay, lower-fired | Fine porcelain clay, higher-fired |
| Water absorption | Up to 7 % (needs sealed grout) | ≤0.5 % (practically waterproof) |
| Hardness / durability | Medium, prone to chipping | High, chip-resistant, good for traffic |
| Weight | Lighter | Denser, heavier |
| Cost per sq ft | $2–$5 | $4–$10+ |
| Typical use | Walls, dry floor areas | Wet floors, showers, outdoors |

So, if your floor will stay dry and budget is tight, ceramic works. If you want a tile that laughs at water and foot traffic, go porcelain.

**Installation tips**
1. **Substrate prep** – Level the subfloor; any bump telegraphs through porcelain especially.
2. **Thinset choice** – Use a polymer-modified thinset rated for porcelain; standard ceramic thinset won’t bond as well.
3. **Grout** – Epoxy grout resists moisture and stains; you’ll get more mileage in a shower.
4. **Cutting** – Ceramic snaps on a manual cutter; porcelain needs a wet saw or diamond blade.
5. **Sealing** – Ceramic grout needs sealing; porcelain grout less so if you pick epoxy.

**Common pitfalls**
- Skipping the primer coat on a slick floor; adhesion drops fast.
- Using cheap spacers; voids in the grout invite water.
- Rushing curing time; walk on porcelain too soon and you’ll chip the edges.

**Manufacturer calibrations**
Reputable brands list water-absorption on the box—look for “PEI” or “ISO 13006” ratings. Anything above PEI 4 is porcelain-grade.

**Testing**
Press a drop of water on the tile back; if it soaks in within thirty seconds, it’s ceramic. If it beads up, you’ve got porcelain.

**Final note**
Porcelain costs more upfront but outlives ceramic in wet, high-traffic zones. Pick based on your budget and where the tile will live.

The short answer: for a shower, epoxy grout is money well spent. The chemistry matters more than the price tag.

Cementitious grout is basically sand and cement. It’s porous, absorbs water, and over time lets moisture creep behind the tile. Epoxy grout is two-part resin that cures into something closer to plastic—no pores, no absorption.

Here’s what that means in a shower:
- Mold resistance: Epoxy won’t feed mold. Cementitious grout stays damp and grows it.
- Stain resistance: Shampoo, soap scum, mineral deposits—epoxy wipes clean. Cementitious holds onto them.
- Flexibility: Epoxy expands and contracts with the tile, so it’s less likely to crack.

The trade-offs:
- Cost: Epoxy runs 3–5 times more than cementitious.
- Application: Epoxy is thick, sets fast, and requires chemical-resistant gloves and speed.
- Cleanup: If you miss a spot, you’re scraping cured epoxy—no easy fix.

If you’re tiling a 36-inch shower wall, epoxy adds maybe $60–$80 to the total material cost. That’s the price of never scrubbing grout lines again.

If you’re on a tight budget, you can compromise: use epoxy in the shower pan and cementitious on the walls, then seal the walls quarterly. But if you want to set it and forget it, go epoxy.

No marble—got it. Glazed ceramic vs porcelain under humidity: porcelain wins every round. Here’s why:

Glazed ceramic is basically clay with a glass-like coating. The glaze itself is non-porous, so water won’t soak through the surface—good for bathroom floors and walls. Fine. You want the hard numbers, not the brochure version. Here’s the real distinction:

**Ceramic** is baked once at around 1,000-1,100°C. Even glazed, the body underneath is still porous clay. Water can soak in through the edges, cracks, or any unglazed contact point. Over time, that moisture migrates into the mortar bed, which can weaken adhesion and cause grout failure.

**Porcelain** is fired at 1,200-1,300°C under higher pressure, producing a denser, vitrified body. The absorption rate drops below 0.5%, meaning water can’t easily penetrate. Even if the glaze chips, the tile body stays mostly dry.

**Practical impact:**  
• If water gets trapped under ceramic tile (say, behind a shower wall or under a floor joint), it stays trapped. That leads to mold, efflorescence, and eventual tile pops.  
• Porcelain won’t absorb that water, so your subfloor stays drier and your installation lasts longer.

**Cost trade-off:** Porcelain is 20-40% more expensive and harder to cut—requires a diamond wet saw with proper water cooling. Ceramic can be snapped with a manual cutter.

**Bottom line:** For a bathroom floor, porcelain is the smarter choice unless you’re on a razor-thin budget and absolutely certain your installation will remain watertight forever. Otherwise, you’re just paying for the trouble later.

For a high-humidity bathroom, your grout choice is basically the difference between a bathroom that lasts decades and one that looks like it’s been attacked by mold spores. Here’s what actually works:

1. Pick the right grout type. Skip non-sanded epoxy if you’re a DIYer—epoxy’s notoriously finicky to mix and set fast. Instead, go with a high-quality sanded urethane grout. It flexes with tile movement, resists cracking, and needs no separate sealer. One coat does both jobs.

2. Match grout color to tiles. Light grout on dark stone shows every speck of dirt; dark grout on light tiles highlights mildew. Pick a shade close to your tile and you’ll cheat the eye into thinking the whole wall is pristine even if it’s not.

3. Texture matters. If your bathroom gets direct steam from a tub or shower, skip the smooth finish and go with a slightly textured grout. The micro-roughness helps the surface stay matte and less inviting to mold.

4. Application technique. Don’t skimp on the float—press grout deep, then wipe clean with a damp sponge before it skins over. Rinse the sponge often so you’re not reapplying mud.

5. Cure time. Give it 24 hours minimum before any water hits it. Humidity in the bathroom will slow curing, so if you live in a coastal place, wait 48.

6. Sealer strategy. If you used urethane, you’re done. If you used cement-based grout (and you shouldn’t, but if you did), apply a penetrating sealer rated for high-moisture areas. Two thin coats beat one thick one every time.

7. Maintenance. Once a month, hit the grout with a spray bottle of vinegar and water. Wipe, don’t scrub. Keeps the microbes down without stripping the seal.

Bottom line: urethane grout, matched color, proper cure, minimal maintenance. That’s the recipe for a bathroom that doesn’t look like a swamp in five years.

7. Maintenance: Keep the floor free of rugs. They block heat, create hot spots, and confuse the sensors.

Fair enough—let’s cut the fluff. The difference comes down to body density and glazing.

Porcelain’s body is fired hotter and tighter, so water can’t soak through the material itself. Ceramic tiles are more porous; water can creep into the body unless it’s fully glazed and the grout stays intact.

A quick kitchen test: flip the tile over, pour water on the back, and wait 15 minutes. If the spot stays dry, you’re looking at porcelain (or fully glazed ceramic). If water beads and disappears, it’s porous ceramic. That’s your floor’s worst-case scenario; if grout fails, porous ceramic will wick water through the tile and you’ll get soft spots under it.

Porcelain wins on raw moisture resistance, but a well-kept ceramic floor with good grout and a proper sealer will also last decades. The real enemy isn’t the tile—it’s bad grout, cracked caulking, and standing water.

Bottom line: pick porcelain if you want zero worries; ceramic works fine if you maintain the grout and seal it every two years. Both will handle a bathroom floor as long as your subfloor and sealant are sound.

A whole roasted chicken is perfect for six people when you add in sides; a 4–4.5 lb bird gives you enough meat with leftovers for sandwiches. Here’s a reliable, forgiving method that keeps the meat juicy and the skin crispy.

### Ingredients (for a 4–4.5 lb chicken)
- 1 whole chicken, neck and giblets removed
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tsp kosher salt per pound of chicken (about 1.5–2 tsp total)
- ½ tsp black pepper
- Optional: 2 tsp smoked paprika, 1 tsp garlic powder
- 1 lemon, halved
- 4–6 sprigs fresh rosemary or thyme
- 2 medium onions, quartered
- 4 carrots, cut into 2-inch chunks
- 3–4 tbsp butter, softened (for basting)

### Equipment
- Roasting pan or heavy skillet with lid
- Meat thermometer
- Kitchen twine (optional, for trussing)
- Cooling rack (helps crispen the bottom skin)

### Prep (15 min)
1. Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C).
2. Pat the chicken dry inside and out with paper towels — this is the secret to crispy skin.
3. Rub olive oil over the skin, then season generously with salt, pepper, and any spices.
4. Stuff the cavity with lemon halves and herb sprigs.
5. Arrange onions and carrots in the pan, place chicken on top. If you like, truss the legs with twine so it cooks evenly.

### Roast (1 hour 20–30 min)
1. Roast uncovered 50–60 minutes. After 30 minutes, baste once with the pan juices or a spoonful of melted butter.
2. Check doneness: thigh temp should read 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part. If the skin browns too fast, tent loosely with foil.
3. Remove chicken to a cutting board, tent with foil, and let rest 15 minutes. Juices redistribute, skin stays crisp.

### Serve
- Carve by separating legs, removing wings, slicing breast across the grain.
- Spoon pan drippings over the meat, serve with roasted carrots and onions.

### Make-ahead tips
- Salt the chicken the night before and refrigerate uncovered; the overnight dry-brine crisps the skin further.
- Roast the chicken at 400°F for slower, more even cooking if you’re serving buffet-style.

### Side suggestions
- Crisp roasted potatoes tossed in the chicken drippings at the last 20 minutes
- Steamed green beans with toasted almonds
- Simple arugula salad with lemon vinaigrette to cut the richness

Perfect plan — Sunday roast chicken is the low-hassle hero of family meals. Here’s a no-fuss method that gives you juicy meat and crisp skin every time.

**Ingredients**
* 1 whole chicken (4.5–5.5 lb), thawed and patted very dry
* 4 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
* 2 tsp coarse kosher salt
* 1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
* 1 tsp garlic powder
* ½ tsp smoked paprika
* 1 lemon, halved
* 1 small bulb garlic, top sliced off
* 3 carrots, cut into 2-inch chunks
* 2 stalks celery, cut into 2-inch pieces
* 2 tbsp olive oil
* ¼ cup dry white wine (optional)

**Method**

1. **Prep the bird:** Remove the chicken from the fridge 30 minutes before roasting. Take the giblet packet out of the cavity and pat the bird dry inside and outside with paper towels — this is the secret to crispy skin.

2. **Make the butter rub:** In a small bowl, mix the softened butter with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and smoked paprika.

3. **Season under the skin:** With clean fingers, gently loosen the skin over the breast and thighs. Rub half the butter mixture directly onto the meat under the skin; smear the rest over the outside of the bird.

4. **Build the roasting bed:** In a roasting pan or Dutch oven, toss the carrots, celery, lemon halves, and garlic bulb with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Place the chicken, breast-side up, on top of the vegetables.

5. **Roast:** Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Roast uncovered for 55–70 minutes, or until a thermometer reads 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh.

6. **Rest and serve:** Transfer the chicken to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and rest 10 minutes. Carve and serve alongside the roasted vegetables and pan juices.

**Tips**
* If you want even more flavor, brush the chicken with the pan juices halfway through cooking.
* The resting step is essential: slicing too soon releases the juices and the meat dries out.
* Use any leftover bones and skin to make a quick stock for tomorrow’s soup.

**Simple Roast Chicken (Serves 6)**  
*One bird, one dish, one pan, zero fuss.*

**Ingredients**
- 1 whole chicken, 4.5–5 lb (about 2.2 kg), thawed if frozen
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 lemon, half juiced, half sliced
- 1 tsp dried thyme (or 1 tbsp fresh)
- 1 tsp dried rosemary (or 2 tbsp fresh)
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- ½ tsp freshly ground black pepper
- 1 onion, quartered
- 2 carrots, cut into 2-inch chunks
- 2 celery stalks, cut into 2-inch chunks
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- ½ cup chicken stock or water

**Equipment**
- Roasting pan (oven-safe, about 10×14 in)
- Tongs
- Meat thermometer (optional but recommended)
- Aluminum foil (optional, for tenting)

---

**Step-by-step**

1. **Prep the bird**  
   Pat the chicken dry inside and out with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

2. **Season**  
   Mix butter, garlic, lemon zest, thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper. Rub half under the skin, half over the outside. Stuff the cavity with lemon slices and any herbs you’ve got.

3. **Prep the pan**  
   Toss onion, carrots, celery with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Spread in the bottom of the roasting pan — this makes a natural rack and keeps the breast off the hot metal.

4. **Roast**  
   Place chicken breast-side up on the veggies. Put the pan in a 425 °F (220 °C) oven. Cook 1 hour, then rotate the pan 180° for even browning.

5. **Check doneness**  
   At 55–60 minutes, check the thigh temperature: 165 °F (74 °C) in the thickest part. If the skin browns too fast, tent loosely with foil.

6. **Rest**  
   Remove the chicken, tent with foil, let rest on a cutting board 10–15 minutes. This keeps the juices inside instead of on the counter.

7. **Finish**  
   Skim fat from the pan juices, add stock, reduce 5 minutes for a quick gravy. Carve, plate, serve.

---

**Quick tips**
- If you want extra-crispy skin, uncover the last 10 minutes and bump the oven to 450 °F.
- For flavor, swap half the stock for white wine or cider.
- Leftovers last 4 days in the fridge; freeze up to 3 months.

Enjoy your Sunday.

**Simple Roast Chicken (Serves 6)**  
*One bird, one dish, one pan, zero fuss.*

**Ingredients**
- 1 whole chicken, 4.5–5 lb (about 2.2 kg), thawed if frozen
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 lemon, half juiced, half sliced
- 1 tsp dried thyme (or 1 tbsp fresh)
- 1 tsp dried rosemary (or 2 tbsp fresh)
- 1 tsp kosher salt
- ½ tsp freshly ground black pepper
- 1 onion, quartered
- 2 carrots, cut into 2-inch chunks
- 2 celery stalks, cut into 2-inch chunks
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- ½ cup chicken stock or water

**Equipment**
- Roasting pan (oven-safe, about 10×14 in)
- Tongs
- Meat thermometer (optional but recommended)
- Aluminum foil (optional, for resting)

**Steps**
1. **Preheat** your oven to 425 °F (220 °C).  
2. **Prep the chicken**: Pat it completely dry with paper towels — this is the secret to crispy skin.  
3. **Season**: Mix the softened butter, garlic, lemon juice, thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper into a paste. Slide it under the skin, especially over the breasts.  
4. **Cavity**: Stuff with lemon slices, onion quarters, and a sprig of rosemary or thyme. Tie legs loosely with kitchen twine (optional).  
5. **Pan**: Place carrots, celery, and onion in the roasting pan, drizzle with olive oil, and scatter around the chicken.  
6. **Roast**: Chicken breast-side up, uncovered, 60–70 minutes. Baste once at the 30-minute mark if you like, but don’t fuss around.  
7. **Check**: Dark meat should hit 175 °F (79 °C), white meat 165 °F (74 °C).  
8. **Rest**: Tent loosely with foil, let sit 10 minutes before carving.  
9. **Serve**: Spoon pan juices over slices. Vegetables roast alongside for free flavor.

**Timing cheat sheet**
- Prep: 10 minutes  
- Oven: 60–70 minutes  
- Rest: 10 minutes  
Total: ~90 minutes, mostly unattended.

**Notes**
- If your oven runs hot, drop to 400 °F (200 °C) and add 10 minutes.  
- Keep a kettle of water nearby — a splash of steam halfway can help crisp the skin without drying the meat.  
- Leftovers? Shred chicken, freeze with pan juices. Great for tacos or soup.

### Herb-Roasted Chicken
**Serves 4–6**

#### What you’ll need
- 1 whole chicken (about 4–5 lb)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
- 2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves
- 1 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped
- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 onion, quartered
- 1 carrot, chopped
- 1 celery stalk, chopped
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper
- Optional: 1 tbsp honey for a subtle glaze

#### Steps
1. **Prep the chicken.** Pat the bird dry inside and out. Season generously inside and out with salt and pepper.
2. **Make the herb mix.** In a small bowl combine the minced garlic, parsley, thyme, rosemary, and olive oil. Slip half of the mixture under the breast skin so it stays moist; rub the rest all over the outside.
3. **Aromatics inside.** Tuck the lemon halves, onion, carrot, and celery into the cavity. They’ll steam the bird from the inside while the skin crisps.
4. **Preheat.** Rack the oven at 400°F (200°C). Tie the legs loosely and tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders so they don’t burn.
5. **Roast.** Place the chicken breast-up on a rack in a roasting pan. Roast 45–55 minutes, or until the thickest part of the thigh hits 165°F.
6. **Baste.** Brush with pan juices or honey every 15 minutes for a lovely sheen.
7. **Rest.** Remove the chicken, tent with foil, and let it sit 10 minutes before carving so the juices redistribute.

#### Quick tips
- If your oven runs hot, drop to 375°F and add 10 minutes.
- For extra crisp skin, broil the last 2–3 minutes, watching closely.
- Swap the herbs for whatever you’ve on hand—this recipe is forgiving.

### Ingredients

Salt and black pepper

### Equipment  
Roasting pan with rack, kitchen twine, meat thermometer

### Prep  
1. **Dry the bird.** Pat the chicken thoroughly with paper towels inside and out; moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.  
2. **Season the cavity.** Stuff the cavity with the lemon halves and the whole head of garlic.

4. **Coat the skin**  
   Rub the remaining butter mixture all over the outside. Pat the skin once more with a paper towel to remove any puddles—thin, even coverage wins.

6. **Roast**

Absolutely, here are the most reliable gluten-free options for a silky gravy:

### Cornstarch
- **How much:** 1 tsp cornstarch per ½ cup liquid (same proportion as flour).
- **Method:** Mix with an equal amount of cold water until smooth, then whisk into the simmering pan.
- **Texture:** Glossy, slightly translucent; does not brown.
- **Tip:** Do not add to boiling liquid or it can turn lumpy; keep the pan at a gentle simmer and stir 1–2 minutes until thickened.

### Arrowroot
- **How much:** 1 tsp per ½ cup liquid.
- **Method:** Slurry first, whisk in, cook 30–60 seconds until glossy.
- **Texture:** Clear, glossy,细腻, very neutral flavor.
- **Tip:** Avoid overcooking; arrowroot breaks down after 5–6 minutes and the gravy thins again.

### Potato Starch
- **How much:** 2 tsp per ½ cup liquid (it’s slightly weaker than cornstarch).
- **Method:** Stir into cold liquid, then combine with hot pan; cook 2–3 minutes.
- **Texture:** Matte finish, slightly thicker body.
- **Tip:** Burns easily; keep heat low and watch the clock.

### Tapioca Starch
- **How much:** 1½ tsp per ½ cup liquid.
- **Method:** Slurry, whisk in, simmer 2–3 minutes until thick.
- **Texture:** Chewy, slightly stretchy; can feel a bit “bouncy.”
- **Tip:** Good for a rustic look; not as silky as cornstarch.

### Xanthan Gum
- **How much:** ¼ tsp per ½ cup liquid (it’s very powerful).
- **Method:** Sprinkle directly into simmering gravy, whisk 30 seconds.
- **Texture:** Smooth, stable; holds up when reheated.
- **Tip:** Use a dab, not a dash; too much makes a gel.

### Quick Decision Guide
- **Speed & shine:** Cornstarch
- **Clear & delicate:** Arrowroot
- **Holds heat best:** Potato starch
- **Stretchy rustic texture:** Tapioca starch
- **Reheats without thinning:** Xanthan gum

### What You’ll Need
- 1 whole chicken (4–5 lb, preferably free-range)
- 2 tbsp olive oil or melted butter
- 1 tsp salt + 1 tsp black pepper
- 1 tsp dried thyme (or 4–5 fresh sprigs)
- 1 lemon, halved (don’t use the whole thing, unless you like puckered flavors)
- 1 medium onion, quartered

### The Plan
1. **Preheat the oven** to 425 °F (220 °C). Line a roasting pan with foil for quick cleanup; nobody wants a scrubbing marathon.
2. **Dry the chicken.** Pat the bird with paper towels until it feels like a desert towel. Moisture is the enemy of crispy skin.
3. **Season it.** Rub the oil or butter all over. Sprinkle salt, pepper, and thyme evenly. Stick the lemon halves, onion, carrot, and celery inside the cavity; they’ll steam the meat from the inside.
4. **Truss the legs.** Tie the legs with kitchen twine so the bird cooks evenly and doesn’t look like it survived a car crash.
5. **Roast.** Place the chicken breast-side up in the pan. Pour the broth around it (not on it). Roast 40–50 minutes until a thermometer reads 165 °F (74 °C) in the thigh.
6. **Rest.** Pull it out, tent with foil, and let it sit 10 minutes. This step is non-negotiable; the juices redistribute and the meat stays moist.

### Side-Dish Synergy
While the chicken rests, you’ve got options:
- **Roasted potatoes:** Toss baby potatoes with oil, salt, rosemary, and roast them in the chicken’s own drippings for 20 minutes.
- **Green beans:** Blanch for 3 minutes, drain, then sauté with garlic and a splash of lemon juice.
- **Simple salad:** Mixed greens, cherry tomatoes, and a vinaigrette. Slice the chicken, plate it, and you’re done.

### Why This Works
The high heat crisps the skin, the cavity vegetables steam the meat, and the resting step locks in moisture. It’s efficient, forgiving, and keeps the kitchen from turning into a battlefield.

**Herb-Roasted Chicken for Eight**  
Serves: 8 (one 5-6 lb bird)  
Total time: 45 min prep, 90–100 min cook  
Active time: 15 min (after you prep)

**Ingredients**  
- 1 whole chicken, 5–6 lb  
- 2 tbsp fresh thyme, chopped  
- 2 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped  
- 1 tbsp fresh sage, chopped (or 1 tsp dried)  
- 1 head garlic, top sliced off, cloves exposed  
- 3 large carrots, peeled, cut into 2-inch chunks  
- 3 large potatoes, cut into 1-inch cubes  
- 1 yellow onion, quartered  
- 3 tbsp olive oil  
- 1 tsp salt  
- ½ tsp black pepper  
- 1 lemon, halved  
- ¼ cup chicken broth (for the pan)

**Method**  
1. **Prep the bird**: Pat the chicken dry inside and out. Season cavity with salt and pepper, then wedge in the lemon halves and half the garlic.  
2. **Herb mix**: In a bowl, combine thyme, rosemary, sage, olive oil, remaining garlic cloves, salt, and pepper. Rub this all over the chicken, including under the skin where possible.  
3. **Build the bed**: Spread carrots, potatoes, and onion on the bottom of a roasting pan. Pour broth over the top.  
4. **Place the bird**: Set the chicken on top, breast side up.  
5. **Roast**: 400°F for 90–100 minutes, until the thigh reaches 165°F and juices run clear.  
6. **Rest & serve**: Let it rest 15 minutes before carving. Skim fat from the pan, deglaze with a splash of broth, and use the liquid as gravy.

**Notes**  
- If you want crispier skin, crank the oven to 450°F for the last 10 minutes.  
- Swap the pan veggies for your family’s favorites—parsnips, sweet potatoes, even halved apples if you’re feeling fancy.  
- Herb crust is optional; if you skip it, just rub with oil and salt. The bird still tastes fine, but you’ll miss the aroma.

**Troubleshooting**  
- **Dry meat?** You’re over-roasting. Stick to 165°F internal temp.  
- **Under-seasoned?** Add a pinch more salt right after resting; chicken absorbs seasoning best at room temp.  
- **No thyme/rosemary/sage?** Use 1 tbsp dried Italian seasoning, but reduce the oil so it doesn’t cake.

### Ingredients (for one 6–7 lb whole chicken)

- 1½ tsp smoked paprika

- 2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves
- 2 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped

- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 onion, quartered
- ½ cup chicken stock or water

### Equipment
- Large roasting pan or Dutch oven
- Kitchen twine
- Digital meat thermometer
- Parchment paper (optional, for easy cleanup)

### Method
1. **Dry the bird**  
   Pat the inside and outside of the chicken bone-dry. Moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

2. **Season cavity**  
   Stuff the cavity with lemon halves and onion quarters. Sprinkle 1 tsp salt inside; this seasons from the inside out.

3. **Make the herb paste**  
   In a small bowl, mix the minced garlic, thyme, rosemary, sage, olive oil, remaining 2 tsp salt, paprika, cumin, and pepper. Mash with a fork until it forms a thick paste.

4. **Loosen the skin**  
   Starting at the breastbone, gently slide your fingers under the skin to create a pocket. Work slowly so it doesn’t tear.

5. **Rub the paste**  
   Spoon most of the herb paste under the skin so it spreads over the breast and thighs. Rub the remaining paste on the outside for color and flavor.

6. **Tie it up**  
   Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine so the bird cooks evenly.

7. **Preheat and roast**  
   Place the chicken breast-side down on a rack in the roasting pan. Add ½ cup stock to the bottom. Roast at 425°F for the first 30 minutes, then flip breast-side up and continue at 375°F until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F—roughly 50–60 minutes total for a 6–7 lb bird.

8. **Rest**  
   Remove the pan from the oven. Let the chicken rest, loosely tented with foil, for 15 minutes. This redistributes the juices so you don’t get dry meat.

9. **Serve**  
   Pour the pan juices into a gravy boat or drizzle over the carved chicken. Serve with roasted root veg or whatever sides your family will actually eat.

### Pro tips
- **Salting ahead** makes a difference. If you can, salt the bird tonight and refrigerate uncovered overnight for deeper seasoning and even crispier skin.
- **Butter basting** is optional. Do NOT add butter to the pan—oil does the job better and you won’t risk burning the garlic.
- **Check early**. Ovens vary; start checking at 50 minutes so you don’t overcook.

### Side-note on fats

**Herb-Roasted Chicken for Eight**  
Serves: 8 (one 5-6 lb bird)  
Total time: 45 min prep, 90–100 min cook

**Ingredients**  
- 1 whole chicken, 5–6 lb, thawed if frozen  
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened  
- 3 tbsp olive oil  
- 1 tbsp grated lemon zest (about one lemon)  
- 1 tbsp lemon juice  
- 4 garlic cloves, minced  
- 2 tsp fresh thyme, chopped  
- 2 tsp fresh rosemary, chopped  
- 1 tsp dried oregano  
- 1 tsp kosher salt (inside cavity)  
- 1 tsp black pepper (inside cavity)  
- ½ tsp cayenne (optional, for heat)  
- 8 sprigs fresh herbs for the cavity (thyme, rosemary, parsley)  
- 1 lemon, halved  
- 1 small onion, quartered  

**Directions**  
1. **Preheat & Prep**  
   Set oven to 425°F. Pull the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead so it thaws evenly. Pat it bone-dry with paper towels—this is non-negotiable for crisp skin.

2. **Make the Herb Paste**  
   In a bowl, mash butter, olive oil, lemon zest, lemon juice, garlic, and the three herbs until it’s a spreadable paste. Season with salt and pepper.

3. **Season the Bird**  
   Loosen the skin over the breast and thighs with your fingers. Slather the herb paste under the skin and over the outside. Toss the cavity with salt, pepper, and cayenne if you want a kick.

4. **Stuff**  
   Stuff the cavity with the herb sprigs, lemon halves, and onion quarters. Tie the legs with kitchen twine.

5. **Roast**  
   Place the chicken on a rack in a roasting pan, breast-side up. Roast 90–100 minutes, or until the thigh thermometer reads 170°F. Baste halfway through with pan juices.

6. **Rest**  
   Pull the bird out and let it rest 20 minutes on a cutting board, loosely tented with foil. This keeps the meat juicy and makes carving easy.

**Serving Tips**  
- Serve with roasted root vegetables (carrots, parsnips, potatoes) tossed in olive oil, salt, and pepper, roasted alongside the chicken for the last 40 minutes.  
- Drizzle pan juices over plates for extra flavor.  
- Garnish with fresh parsley and lemon wedges.

**Troubleshooting**  
- Skin not crispy? Ensure the chicken is bone-dry before roasting and skip covering it in foil.  
- Meat dry? Check temperature early; pull at 170°F, not 180°F, and rest fully.  
- Flavor bland? Boost the herb paste with an extra clove of garlic or a pinch of smoked paprika.

### Ingredients (for one 6–7 lb whole chicken)
- 1 whole chicken, rinsed and patted bone-dry
- 3 tsp kosher salt (divided)
- 1½ tsp smoked paprika
- 1 tsp ground cumin
- ½ tsp black pepper
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves
- 2 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped
- 2 tbsp fresh sage, chopped
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 onion, quartered
- ½ cup chicken broth or water

### Equipment
- Large roasting pan or Dutch oven
- Kitchen twine
- Digital meat thermometer
- Parchment paper (optional, for easy cleanup)

### Method
1. **Dry the bird**  
   Pat the inside and outside of the chicken bone-dry. Moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

2. **Season cavity**  
   Stuff the cavity with lemon halves and onion quarters. Sprinkle 1 tsp salt inside; this seasons from the inside out.

3. **Make the herb paste**  
   In a small bowl, mix the minced garlic, thyme, rosemary, sage, olive oil, remaining 2 tsp salt, paprika, cumin, and pepper. Mash with a fork until it forms a thick paste.

4. **Loosen the skin**  
   Starting at the breastbone, gently slide your fingers under the skin to create a pocket. Work slowly so it doesn’t tear.

5. **Rub the paste**  
   Spoon most of the herb paste under the skin so it spreads over the breast and thighs. Rub the remaining paste on the outside for color and flavor.

6. **Tie it up**  
   Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine so the bird cooks evenly.

7. **Preheat and roast**  
   Place the chicken breast-side down on a rack in the roasting pan. Add broth to the bottom.  
   Roast at 425°F for 15 minutes, then reduce to 375°F and continue for 50–60 minutes.

8. **Check doneness**  
   Insert the thermometer into the thickest part of the thigh; it should read 165°F. If unsure, pull a leg—it should move easily.

9. **Rest**  
   Remove from the oven, tent with foil, and rest 15 minutes before carving. The juices redistribute; the meat stays juicy.

### Quick Fixes if Things Go Wrong
- **Skin still soggy?** Crank the broiler for the last 3 minutes, but stand by—the skin will char fast.
- **Dry breast?** Tent foil halfway through; the breast cooks faster than the legs.
- **Dry legs?** Remove them when they hit 165°F, let the breast finish. Everyone gets tender meat.

### Serving

## Timeline for a 7:00 PM Sit-Down

**3:30 PM – Chill the Chicken**  
Place the chicken in a roasting pan, refrigerate uncovered so the skin dries out. While it chills, wash your hands and prep the herb rub ingredients.

**4:15 PM – Prepare the Vegetables**  
While the chicken rests in the cold, peel and cut the rutabaga into 1-inch cubes. Toss with oil, ginger, honey, salt, and pepper, then spread on a rimmed baking sheet. Refrigerate for 20 minutes to let flavors meld.

**5:00 PM – Herb the Chicken**  
Take the chicken out of the fridge, pat dry, and rub the herb mixture under the breast skin and over the breast. Tuck lemon and garlic inside, truss legs, and return to the counter.

**5:30 PM – Preheat and Slide In**  
Turn the oven to 425 °F. Slide both the chicken pan and rutabaga tray in at the same time, chicken on the top rack, rutabaga below.

**6:25 PM – Check and Adjust**  
The rutabaga will be nearly done; the chicken still needs time. Keep an eye on the skin color—tent foil if it browns too fast.

**6:50 PM – Finish Vegetables**  
Remove the rutabaga, sprinkle any sesame seeds if using, and set them on a warm plate. The chicken will hit 165 °F in the next 5–10 minutes.

**7:00 PM – Rest Chicken, Serve**  
Pull the chicken, rest 10 minutes, then carve. Reheat the rutabaga in the microwave for 30 seconds if needed, and serve alongside the chicken.

## Dessert Prep While Chicken Rests

**6:45 PM – Assemble Dessert**  
While the chicken rests, make a simple no-bake dessert like chocolate-dipped fruit skewers or espresso-poached pears. These finish in under 10 minutes and need no extra oven space.

**7:00 PM – Table Ready**  
Chicken, rutabaga, and dessert all ready. Invite the family to the table.

Fine. Crispy skin on a roast chicken is basically physics: you want dry surface, high heat, and nothing steaming the skin. Here’s the short version that actually works.

1. **Bird** – Pick a 4–5 lb free-range chicken; bigger birds give juicier meat without drying out.

2. **Dry it** – Pat the skin bone-dry with paper towels. Leave it uncovered in the fridge 24 h (plastic-wrapped loosely, skin side up). The skin dries out and crisps like a chip.

3. **Season** – Salt under the skin (about 1 tsp on breast, 1 tsp on thighs) so the meat tastes seasoned. Lightly oil the skin and add black pepper or thyme if you like.

4. **Truss** – Tie legs together and tuck wing tips under. Keeps the bird compact and cooks evenly.

5. **Rack it** – Put the chicken on a wire rack set in a roasting pan. Air circulates under the skin, no soggy bottom.

6. **Heat** – Preheat oven to 220 °C / 425 °F. Start hot to brown the skin, then drop to 180 °C / 350 °F for the rest of the cook.

7. **Roast** – 20 min at high, then turn down and roast 20 min per pound. Check at 1.5 h; insert a probe into the thickest thigh meat—165 °F / 74 °C means done.

8. **Rest** – Pull it out, tent with foil, let it rest 15 min. Meat redistributes juices, skin stays crisp.

Optional but helpful:
- **Butter** – Rub 2 tbsp softened butter under the skin for flavor; it won’t stop crisping if the skin is dry first.
- **Veggies** – Toss carrots, parsnips, and onions in the pan; their juices baste the chicken as it roasts.
- **Brine** – If you forget the overnight dry, use a 10 % salt water brine for 1 h, then dry again.

**Roast Chicken for Six**

*Ingredients*
- One whole chicken, 5–5.5 lb (2.25–2.5 kg)
- 4 tbsp unsalted butter, softened (or olive oil if you want vegetarian-friendly)
- 1 head garlic, top sliced off, cloves exposed
- 1 lemon, halved
- 2 sprigs fresh thyme, plus extra for stuffing
- 3 sprigs fresh rosemary, plus extra for stuffing
- 1 tsp salt (plus more for cavity)
- ½ tsp black pepper
- 1 cup chicken stock
- 1 small onion, thickly sliced
- 1 carrot, thickly sliced

*Equipment*
- 12-inch oven-safe skillet or roasting pan
- Kitchen twine or a roaster rack

*Instructions*
1. **Prep the bird**
   - Preheat oven to 425 °F (220 °C).
   - Pat the chicken dry inside and out; a dry skin equals crispy skin.
   - Season inside the cavity with salt and pepper. Toss in the garlic head, lemon halves, and extra thyme/rosemary sprigs for steam-flavor.
   - Tie the legs with twine and tuck the wing tips under the body so they roast evenly.

2. **Season the skin**
   - Mix the butter with the remaining salt, pepper, and chopped herbs.
   - Rub the mixture under and over the skin, working it gently so the flavors migrate.

3. **Roast**
   - Place the chicken breast-side up in the skillet or roasting pan.
   - Scatter onion and carrot around the bird; they’ll caramelize and become a base for gravy.
   - Roast 1 ½–2 hours, basting once at the 45-minute mark, until the thigh reaches 165 °F (74 °C) and juices run clear.

4. **Rest**
   - Transfer the bird to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and let it rest 20 minutes. This redistributes the juices and keeps the meat moist.

5. **Make the pan jus**
   - While the chicken rests, pour off excess fat, skim the top, and whisk in the chicken stock.
   - Simmer on the stovetop 3–5 minutes until it reduces to a glossy glaze; strain if you want it silky smooth.

**Serving Idea**  
Carve the chicken and serve with the jus drizzled over the top. The roasted vegetables and caramelized garlic can be mashed into a quick sauce or scattered alongside.

*Tips*  
- If you don’t have fresh herbs, use 2 tsp dried thyme and 1 tsp dried rosemary (reduce the salt by ½ tsp).  
- For extra crispy skin, broil the chicken for the last 3 minutes, watching closely to prevent burning.

### Roast Chicken for Six

**Ingredients**  
1 whole chicken (5–5.5 lb / 2.3–2.5 kg)  
2 Tbsp unsalted butter, softened  
3 cloves garlic, minced  
1 tsp each: smoked paprika, dried thyme, salt  
½ tsp black pepper  
1 lemon, halved  
1 onion, cut into wedges  
2 small carrots, cut into 2-inch pieces  
4 sprigs fresh rosemary  
1 cup dry white wine (or chicken stock)  
1 Tbsp olive oil  

### Method  

**1. Prep the chicken**  
Pat the bird thoroughly dry inside and out with paper towels — this is the secret to crisp skin. Score the breast skin lightly with a sharp knife so the seasoning gets underneath.

**2. Seasoning paste**  
Mix the softened butter with garlic, smoked paprika, thyme, salt, and pepper. Slide this paste under the skin all over the breast, and rub the rest on the outside.

**3. Stuff and truss**  
Toss the onion wedges, carrot pieces, and one lemon half into the cavity. Tie the legs together with kitchen twine; tuck the wing tips behind the back so they roast evenly.

**4. Roasting setup**  
Arrange the remaining lemon half, onion wedges, and carrots in a 9×13-inch roasting pan. Place the chicken on top, skin-side up, and drizzle with olive oil. Scatter rosemary around.

**5. Roast**  
Roast at 425 °F (220 °C) for 1 hour, then reduce to 375 °F (190 °C) for another 45 minutes. Pour the wine into the pan halfway through; it will create steam and later become the base of your gravy.

**6. Check doneness**  
Pull the chicken when the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165 °F (74 °C) or when juices run clear.

**7. Rest**  
Transfer to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and let rest 15 minutes. This keeps the meat juicy and makes carving easier.

**8. Serve**  
Carve against the grain and serve with the pan juices spooned over. The vegetables underneath roast into soft, caramelized bits that pair beautifully with the chicken.

### Notes  
- If you don't have a roasting rack, prop the chicken on the vegetables — they act as a natural rack while absorbing flavor.  
- For extra basting, spoon the pan juices over the chicken every 20 minutes during the first hour.  
- Leftovers make great chicken salad or sandwiches; the skin crisps up again when reheated in a skillet.

**Roast chicken for six, done right the first time**

1. **The bird** – Pick a 4 lb (1.8 kg) chicken, skin intact, no weird cuts or “spatchcock” nonsense. Thaw it overnight if frozen, then pat it bone-dry with paper towels. Dry skin equals crispy skin, and we’re not negotiating.

2. **Seasoning** – You’ll need salt, pepper, and whatever fresh herb the supermarket has. Mix 1 tbsp kosher salt, 2 tsp black pepper, and two handfuls of roughly chopped parsley (or rosemary if you’re fancy). Rub it all over the chicken, including under the breast skin; that’s where the flavor lives.

3. **Oven** – Preheat to 425 °F (220 °C). Rack in the center, roasting pan or rimmed baking sheet greased with a touch of oil or butter. Chicken goes in breast-side up.

4. **Cooking** – Set a 30-minute timer. After those 30 minutes, check the internal temp at the thickest part of the thigh (not the breast; breast cooks faster). You want 170 °F (77 °C). If it’s not there, give it 5–7 more minutes and recheck.

5. **Rest** – Pull the chicken out, tent it loosely with foil, and let it sit 10 minutes on the counter. This lets the juices finish distributing so the meat stays moist.

6. **Carving** – Cut the legs off first, then the wings, then slice the breast against the grain. Serve with whatever vegetables you can boil in the same 30 minutes (potatoes, carrots, green beans).

**Tools you actually need**
- Instant-read thermometer (digital is fine; it saves you from guesswork)
- Sharp carving knife
- Rimmed baking sheet or roasting pan
- Foil
- Paper towels

**Common mistakes to avoid**
- Do NOT stuff the cavity with lemon or onion; it steams the skin and you’ll lose crispness.
- Do NOT baste; opening the oven door drops the temperature and extends cook time.
- Do NOT over-salt; kosher salt is fluffy, so eyeballing is fine, but don’t go overboard.

**Flavor upgrades**
- Swap parsley for thyme if you like earthier notes.
- Add a tablespoon of smoked paprika to the rub for a subtle smoky kick.
- Drizzle with a splash of lemon juice right before serving if you want brightness.

**Timing cheat sheet**
- Prep: 10 minutes
- Cook: 30–40 minutes
- Rest: 10 minutes
- Total: 1 hour

Here’s a roast chicken that actually stays moist and won’t fall apart. Six hungry people, one bird, done by six-thirty.

**The bird:** 4.5 to 5 lb whole chicken, skin still on.  
**The oven:** 425 °F, rack in the lower third so the bottom crisps.  
**Time:** 90 minutes total, 25 minutes to prep, 65 minutes in the oven.

**Ingredients**  
- 1 whole chicken, thawed  
- 4 tbsp unsalted butter, softened  
- 1 lemon, half sliced thin, half juiced  
- 6 garlic cloves, smashed  
- 1 bunch fresh thyme (about 10 sprigs)  
- 1 bunch fresh rosemary (about 6 sprigs)  
- 1 tsp kosher salt plus extra for the cavity  
- ½ tsp black pepper  
- 1 onion, quartered  
- 2 carrots, cut into sticks  
- 1 cup chicken broth  
- 1 sprig parsley, leaves stripped plus 1 sprig for garnish  

**Method**  
1. Preheat the oven to 425 °F.  
2. Pat the chicken completely dry; moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.  
3. Mix the softened butter with minced garlic, zest from the lemon, and the chopped herbs.  
4. Loosen the skin over the breast with your fingers, then rub half the herb butter under it and the rest on top.  
5. Season the cavity with salt, pepper, and the remaining lemon slices and garlic.  
6. Place the onion and carrots in a roasting pan, pour in broth, and set the chicken on top.  
7. Roast 60–65 minutes, basting once at the 40-minute mark, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165 °F.  
8. Tent with foil and let rest 15 minutes; the juices will redistribute and the skin will stay crisp.  
9. Carve, serve, and garnish with fresh parsley.

**What to watch**  
- If the skin browns too fast, tent loosely with foil after 30 minutes.  
- Use a meat thermometer; guesswork yields dry meat.  
- If you want extra crisp, skip the tent and turn the heat up the last ten minutes.

**Flavor boosters**  
Swap the lemon for orange if you like citrus brighter than tart.  
Add a pinch of smoked paprika to the butter for a subtle warmth.  
Finish with a drizzle of honey for a sweet glaze if the kitchen feels like a carnival.

**Make-ahead tips**  
Butter and herbs can be mixed a day ahead and refrigerated.  
Stuff the cavity the night before; just let the bird sit uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry the skin.  
Everything else assembles in fifteen minutes on Sunday.

**Leftover strategy**  
Store meat and bones separately in the fridge for four days.  
Shred the chicken, toss with a splash of pan drippings and Dijon, and you’ve got sandwiches for lunch.  
Simmer the carcass with water, onion, carrot, and bay leaf; strain for stock that’ll turn a simple soup into something worth talking about.

That’s it. No fuss, no drama, no garbage. Just a chicken that actually tastes like something you paid for.

- 20 min: Potatoes in

3. **Season generously**. Rub 2 Tbsp salt and 1 tsp pepper all over, inside the cavity, and under the breast skin. Add 1 tsp dried thyme if you like. Leave the skin intact and don’t oil it yet—that early oil can scorch.

4. **Truss or not**. Skewer or tie the legs together if you want a tidy shape. If you’re lazy and don’t mind uneven legs, skip it; the bird will still cook.

5. **Place on a rack in a roasting pan**. The rack lifts the chicken so air circulates beneath; otherwise the bottom steams.

6. **Roast 45–55 minutes**. Check at 45; when a meat thermometer in the thickest thigh reads 165 °F, it’s done. If it’s still pink, give it another five.

7. **Rest ten minutes**. Transfer to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil. Resting holds the juices so they don’t gush out when you carve.

8. **Make pan gravy**. Dump the fat from the pan into a saucepan, leave 1 Tbsp in the roaster. Stir in 2 Tbsp flour, cook 1 minute, whisk in 1 cup broth, simmer until thick. Season to taste.

9. **Carve and serve**. Slice breast meat on the bias, split the legs at the joint, wing off at the first knuckle.

10. **Cleanup tip**. If the roaster’s stuck on, soak in hot soapy water for 10 minutes, scrape with a wooden spoon.

One more thing: if you’re short on time, a 4 lb bird at 425 °F is usually done in 45 minutes. Trust the thermometer, not the clock.

**Roast Chicken with Herbs & Root Vegetables**

*Ingredients*

• 1 whole chicken (1.5–2 kg), giblets removed  
• 2 tbsp olive oil, plus extra for brushing  
• 2 tsp chopped fresh rosemary  
• 2 tsp chopped fresh thyme  
• 2 cloves garlic, minced  
• 1 tsp paprika (smoked adds depth)  
• 1 kg mixed root vegetables (carrots, parsnips, potatoes), peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks  
• 2 onions, quartered  
• 250 ml chicken stock  
• Salt and pepper to taste  

*Method*

1. Preheat the oven to 200 °C (180 °C fan).  
2. Pat the chicken dry inside and out; this helps the skin crisp. Rub the cavity and skin with olive oil, then season generously with salt and pepper.  
3. Mix the herbs, garlic, and paprika with a little oil to make a paste and spread it under the skin on the breast, then over the breast meat.  
4. Place the chicken on a rack in a roasting tin. Scatter the vegetables and onion around the base.  
5. Pour the stock into the tin.  
6. Roast for 50–60 minutes, basting every 20 minutes with the pan juices. The skin should be golden and the juices clear when the thickest part of the thigh is pierced.  
7. Remove the chicken to a board, cover loosely with foil, and rest for 10–15 minutes—this keeps the meat juicy.  
8. Meanwhile, give the vegetables a quick blast under the grill for 2–3 minutes for extra colour if you like.

Carve the chicken and serve with the roasted vegetables and a drizzle of the pan juices. Works beautifully with a glass of chilled rosé or a pot of Yorkshire puddings if you’re feeling fancy.

*Storage*

Leftovers keep for three days in the fridge. Keep the meat and juices separate for reheating; microwave the veg gently and warm the meat in a low oven. Freeze portions of meat with stock in airtight containers for up to two months.

Making gluten-free gravy from chicken drippings is easy once you know the right thickener. Here are two reliable methods:

**Roux-based (Cornstarch or Arrowroot)**
1. Pour the pan drippings into a saucepan and skim off excess fat.
2. Whisk in 1 tbsp cornstarch (or 1.5 tbsp arrowroot powder) per cup of stock.
3. Add 1 cup chicken stock, whisk constantly, and simmer 3–5 minutes until thick.
4. Season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of thyme.

**Tahini-based (Nut-free, dairy-free)**
1. Skim drippings, then whisk 2 tbsp tahini with 1 cup stock.
2. Simmer 4–5 minutes; the gravy thickens naturally without a starch.
3. Add salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lemon for brightness.

Both methods stay gluten-free and work with the same roasting pan juices. Cornstarch gives a glossy sheen; arrowroot is clearer and more neutral. Tahini adds a mild nutty note but no gluten or dairy.

**Avoid** flour or wheat-based blends—those are the usual culprits for hidden gluten. And skip the old trick of adding soy sauce for color; even “gluten-free” soy sauce often contains barley or wheat derivatives and can introduce gluten cross-contact. Just stick with pure thickeners and you’ll have a safe, delicious gravy.

You can still pull together a rich, glossy gravy without any wheat — the chicken drippings already have plenty of flavor, you just need a gluten-free thickener. Here are three tried-and-true options, from easiest to most rustic.

### 1. Cornstarch Slurry (Fastest)
* Makes a silky, translucent gravy
1. Skim most of the fat from the roasting pan, leaving 2–3 tbsp.  
2. Return the pan to medium heat, add ½ cup chicken stock or water, scrape up the brown bits.  
3. In a small bowl whisk 1 tbsp cornstarch with 2 tbsp cold water until smooth.  
4. Stir the slurry into the simmering liquid, bring to a gentle boil, and cook 2 minutes until thickened.  
5. Season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of thyme.

### 2. Potato Starch (Neutral Flavor, Thick)
* Works like cornstarch but gives a slightly denser texture
1. Use the same base as above, but swap cornstarch for potato starch.  
2. Reduce liquid a touch (use ¼ cup stock + ¼ cup water) so the gravy isn’t too thin.  
3. Bring to a boil, whisk in 1 tbsp potato starch mixed with 2 tbsp cold water; simmer 2 minutes.

### 3. Roux-Free Grain Blend (Whole-Food Option)
* Adds body and a nutty note
1. Roast 2 tbsp rice flour and 1 tbsp tapioca flour in the pan fat until lightly toasted (3–4 minutes).  
2. Whisk in ½ cup stock gradually, scraping the bottom.  
3. Simmer 5 minutes until thickened; finish with a pat of butter for gloss.

### Quick Tips
• If the gravy is too thin, add another half-teaspoon of starch slurry; too thick, dilute with a splash of stock.  
• Always whisk while adding the thickener to keep it smooth.  
• For extra richness, whisk in 1 tsp Dijon mustard off the heat right before serving.

Making gluten-free gravy with chicken drippings is actually quite straightforward. The key is swapping out wheat flour for a gluten-free starch and using the natural fat and flavor already in your roasting pan. Here’s a simple, flavorful method:

**Gluten-Free Roast Chicken Gravy**

*Ingredients*
- 2 tbsp gluten-free all-purpose flour (rice, sorghum, or tapioca blend)
- 2 tbsp olive oil or chicken fat from the drippings
- 1 small onion, minced (optional, for depth)
- 2 cups low-sodium chicken stock
- ½ cup reserved pan drippings (fat + juices)
- 1 tsp fresh thyme leaves
- Salt and pepper to taste

*Steps*
1. **Skim the fat:** After you remove the chicken, pour the pan drippings into a heatproof measuring cup. Let it settle for a minute; the fat will rise to the top. Skim off about 2 tablespoons of fat and reserve the rest. You’ll use the fat to make a roux and keep the flavorful juices for the gravy.
2. **Make the roux:** In the same roasting pan, heat the reserved drippings (or olive oil if you skimmed most of the fat) over medium heat. Sprinkle in the gluten-free flour and whisk continuously for 2–3 minutes until it turns golden and smells slightly nutty. This step removes any raw starch taste.
3. **Add aromatics:** Toss in the minced onion and cook for another minute until soft. This adds sweetness and rounds out the flavor.
4. **Deglaze:** Pour in the reserved pan juices and scrape up any browned bits stuck to the bottom—they’re packed with flavor.
5. **Simmer the stock:** Slowly pour in the chicken stock while whisking to keep the roux lump-free. Add the thyme leaves and bring to a gentle simmer.
6. **Thicken:** Let the gravy simmer for 5–7 minutes, stirring occasionally. It should coat the back of a spoon. If it’s too thick, add more stock; if too thin, simmer a bit longer or whisk in a teaspoon of cornstarch slurry.
7. **Finish and season:** Season with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust—sometimes the pan juices have enough salt, so add gradually.

*Notes*
- If you don’t have gluten-free flour on hand, cornstarch works too: whisk 1 tablespoon cornstarch with 2 tablespoons cold water and stir it into the simmering stock in step 6. It thickens faster and gives a glossy finish.
- For extra richness, stir in a tablespoon of butter just before serving.
- If you like a deeper, smokier flavor, add a pinch of smoked paprika or a splash of Worcestershire (check that it’s gluten-free).

**How to do it**
1. **Prep the chicken:** Pat the bird dry inside and out. Mix the softened butter with the thyme, rosemary, salt, and pepper. Slip half of that mixture under the breast skin, then rub the rest all over the outside. Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders and truss the legs with kitchen string.

- Cook: 1 hour 20 minutes total
- Rest: 15 minutes
- Total: about 1 hour 50 minutes

Here’s a tried-and-true Sunday roast chicken recipe that’s flavorful, forgiving, and impressive without being fussy.

**Ingredients**
- 2 whole chickens (3–4 lb each)
- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 bulb of garlic, top sliced off
- 1 head of fennel or small bunch of thyme (optional)
- 3 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 2 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped
- 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- 1 tsp salt (plus more for cavity)
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- 1 tbsp olive oil

**Tools**
- Roasting pan (large enough for two birds side by side)
- Kitchen twine or skewers
- Instant-read thermometer

**Method**

1. **Prep the chicken:** Remove giblets and pat birds dry inside and out. Truss legs with kitchen twine (helps them cook evenly and keeps the shape). Place lemon halves, garlic, and herbs in the cavity.

2. **Season:** Mix butter, paprika, chopped rosemary, thyme, salt, and pepper. Slide this mixture under the skin of the breast and thighs, massaging gently so it coats the meat.

3. **Arrange:** Sit the chickens on a rack in the roasting pan. Brush skin with olive oil and season lightly with salt and pepper.

4. **Roast:** Preheat oven to 425°F. Insert the pan and roast for 45–55 minutes until the internal temp at the thickest part of the thigh hits 170°F.

5. **Rest:** Pull from oven and let the birds rest 15 minutes before carving. This keeps the meat moist and makes slicing cleaner.

While the chicken rests, the pan drippings are gold for gravy. Tilt the pan, skim off excess fat, and add 1 tbsp flour and 1 cup chicken stock to make a quick pan sauce (optional).

**Serving and sides**

Carve each chicken into 4–5 portions (two breasts, two thighs, one wing each). Serve with:

- Roasted baby potatoes (tossed in same pan after chicken is out)
- Sautéed green beans with garlic and lemon zest
- Warm dinner rolls for mopping up pan drippings
- Simple green salad with vinaigrette

**Tips for success**

- Make sure the oven is fully preheated before sliding the pan in.
- Use an instant-read thermometer; timing varies by oven and bird size.
- If you’re short on time, skip trussing — just lay the birds flat and rotate the pan halfway through.

Bring a bottle of your favorite wine, set the table simply, and let the aroma of rosemary and lemon do most of the entertaining. Enjoy your dinner!

Ingredients

### Hearty Wild-Rice & Mushroom Pilaf
Wild rice has a nutty, meaty flavor that holds up beside roast chicken, and it’s naturally gluten-free. Mushrooms add umami without any dairy needed.

**What you need**
* 1 cup wild rice (or a 50/50 mix of wild and brown rice)
* 2½ cups low-sodium chicken stock
* 8 oz cremini mushrooms, sliced
* 1 small onion, diced
* 2 cloves garlic, minced
* 2 tbsp butter or olive oil
* 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves
* ½ tsp salt, ¼ tsp pepper
* 1 tbsp sherry vinegar (optional, for brightness)

**How to make it**
1. Rinse the rice, then simmer in the stock covered for 35–40 minutes until tender but still chewy.
2. While rice cooks, sauté onion in butter/oil until soft; add mushrooms and thyme, cook until liquid evaporates.
3. Stir garlic in the last minute, taste for salt/pepper.
4. When rice is done, fluff it, fold in the mushroom mixture, and finish with a splash of vinegar if you like a little lift.

**Why it works**
The stock seasons the rice deeply so it never tastes bland, and the mushrooms provide that “creamy” mouth-feel without any cream. Serve alongside the chicken and you’ll have a plate that feels festive, but the prep is almost entirely one-pot.

## Roast Chicken with Herbs and Lemon

### Ingredients
- 1 whole chicken (about 3.5–4 lbs / 1.6–1.8 kg)
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 1 lemon, halved
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped
- 1 tbsp fresh thyme, chopped
- 1 tsp fresh sage, chopped
- 1 tsp salt
- ½ tsp black pepper
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 onion, quartered
- 3 carrots, roughly chopped
- 2 celery stalks, roughly chopped
- 2 cups chicken stock

### Equipment
- Roasting pan or baking dish
- Kitchen twine
- Meat thermometer

### Method

1. **Prep the chicken**  
   Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C). Pat the chicken dry inside and out with paper towels — this is the secret to crispy skin. Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders and tie the legs together with kitchen twine.

2. **Season under the skin**  
   Gently loosen the skin over the breast with your fingers. Mix the softened butter with minced garlic, herbs, salt, and pepper. Slide half the mixture under the skin, then rub the rest all over the outside.

3. **Stuff the cavity**  
   Place two lemon halves and leftover herbs inside the cavity. This keeps the bird moist and infuses flavor as it cooks.

4. **Arrange the vegetables**  
   Toss the onion, carrots, and celery with olive oil and a pinch of salt. Scatter them in the roasting pan — they’ll make a natural rack and flavor the pan juices.

5. **Roast**  
   Place the chicken breast-side up on the vegetables. Pour the chicken stock into the pan (not the bird). Roast for 1½ hours, or until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C).

6. **Rest and serve**  
   Transfer the chicken to a cutting board, tent loosely with foil, and let rest 15 minutes. This keeps the juices inside. Carve and serve with the roasted vegetables and pan juices spooned over.

### Tips
- Don’t cover the chicken while resting — the skin will stay crisp.
- If the skin browns too fast, tent with foil for the last 30 minutes.
- Save the carcass for stock: simmer with onion, carrot, celery, and herbs for 2–3 hours, strain, and freeze in portions.

This recipe feeds 4–6 and reheats well — leftovers make great sandwiches. Enjoy your dinner!

Cook 3 cups water with 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tsp salt, stir in 1½ cups couscous, cover, and let stand 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork and stir in ¼ cup fresh lemon juice and 2 tbsp chopped mint. The citrus brightens the meal.

Got it — absolutely no cornstarch. Let’s pivot to clean, corn-free thickeners that keep the pan gravy silky and the family safe.

**Option 1: Arrowroot powder**
Arrowroot is the closest 1:1 swap. Use 2 teaspoons for the same 1 tablespoon cornstarch. Whisk it into 2 tablespoons cold stock, then stir into the hot drippings. It thickens fast, stays glossy, and tastes neutral. Works beautifully with chicken.

**Option 2: Potato starch**
Potato starch behaves like cornstarch but without the corn. Use the same 1:1 ratio. Sprinkle it into the pan drippings, whisk, and simmer 2 minutes. The sauce stays clear and doesn’t gum up like flour can.

**Option 3: Roux with rice flour**
Rice flour is naturally GF and corn-free. Melt 1 tablespoon butter in the roasting pan, whisk in 1 tablespoon rice flour, cook 1 minute until it smells toasty. Then whisk in 1 cup stock, simmer until thick. The flavor is nutty but mild; it pairs well with roast chicken.

**Option 4: Reduction**
Skip the starch altogether. Skim the fat from the pan drippings, bring the liquid to a boil, and reduce it by half. The natural collagen in the drippings will thicken it into a glossy, intensely flavored sauce. Add a splash of stock if it gets too thick.

**Option 5: Beurre monté**
For a luxurious finish, whisk cold butter cubes into your reduced drippings off the heat. The sauce becomes emulsified, velvety, and glossy without any starch. Just don’t let it boil or it’ll split.

My top pick: arrowroot if you want speed, or reduction if you want depth and simplicity. Both are completely corn-free.

**Ingredients**
- 1 whole chicken, 4–5 lb (about 2–2.25 kg)
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened
- 1 tbsp fresh thyme leaves (or 1 tsp dried)
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 onion, quartered
- 1 cup dry white wine (optional; swap for chicken broth)
- 2 tsp salt, divided
- 1 tsp black pepper
- 2 carrots, cut into chunks
- 1 parsnip, cut into chunks
- 2–3 potatoes, quartered
- Olive oil for roasting pan

- Large roasting pan
- Meat thermometer
- Aluminum foil

1. **Prep the chicken**
   - Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C).

Got it — no cornstarch. That’s easy to work around; there are plenty of corn-free alternatives that still give you a glossy, velvety gravy. Here are the best options, plus how to use them without messing with the flavour of your roast.

### 1. Arrowroot powder (1:1 swap)
- **Why it works:** It’s a pure starch from the arrowroot plant, gives a clear shine, and sets quickly at a boil.  
- **How to use:** Mix 1 tbsp arrowroot with 2 tbsp cold water or stock to make a smooth slurry. Stir into simmering gravy and cook 1–2 minutes until glossy.  
- **Bonus:** It won’t break down if you reheat leftovers, unlike cornstarch which can go grainy.

### 2. Potato starch (1:1 swap)
- **Why it works:** Made from potatoes, so it’s naturally corn-free and gives a soft, silky mouthfeel.  
- **How to use:** Same slurry method as arrowroot — 1 tbsp starch to 2 tbsp cold liquid. Add to pan, bring to a gentle boil, and stir until thickened.  
- **Tip:** Don’t overcook; potato starch can thin out again if you keep it on high heat.

### 3. Tapioca starch (1:1 swap)
- **Why it works:** Native to the cassava root, tapioca gives a slightly glossy finish and holds well in acidic sauces.  
- **How to use:** Whisk 1 tbsp tapioca with 2 tbsp cold water or stock. Stir into your pan juices and simmer until thickened.  
- **Note:** Some brands are processed on shared lines with corn, so check the label if your allergy is severe.

### 4. Beurre manié (1 tbsp butter + 1 tbsp flour)
- **Why it works:** Classic French technique — equal parts softened butter and all-purpose flour kneaded together.  
- **How to use:** Add small knobs to the simmering gravy and whisk until melted and thickened. Cook 2–3 minutes to remove the raw flour taste.  
- **Benefit:** Adds richness and a nutty depth that pairs beautifully with roast chicken.

### 5. Roux (1 tbsp butter + 1 tbsp flour cooked first)
- **Why it works:** The butter and flour are cooked together before adding liquid, which eliminates the raw flour flavour and gives a deeper flavour base.  
- **How to use:** Melt butter in a small pan, add flour, cook 2 minutes until pale gold. Whisk in stock or milk gradually, then pour into your main pan.  
- **Pro tip:** Cook the roux a minute longer for a slightly toasted note that complements roasted vegetables.

### 6. Lentil flour (1 tbsp per cup of liquid)
- **Why it works:** Red lentils break down into a fine, nutty flour that thickens without any starch.  
- **How to use:** Blend dry red lentils until powdery, then whisk into simmering stock. Cook 3–4 minutes until the gravy thickens naturally.  
- **Bonus:** Adds a subtle earthy sweetness and a boost of protein.

### How to choose
- **For quickest results:** Arrowroot or potato starch slurry — just mix and stir.  
- **For richest flavour:** Beurre manié or roux — you’ll get a deeper roast profile.  
- **For allergen-conscious kitchens:** Stick with arrowroot or potato starch, which are naturally corn-free and less likely to be cross-contaminated.

### 1. Start with the dessert (the one that likes to chill)

- Simmer 2–3 minutes until glossy.  
- **Timing:** This happens while the chicken rests 10 minutes, so nothing sits idle.

### 6. Finish and plate
- Carve the chicken, plate with potatoes and beans, pour gravy over the top.

Roasting tin, baking sheet, kitchen twine, sharp knife, meat thermometer

### Step-by-step

**1. Prep the chicken**  
- Pat the chicken dry with paper towels — this helps the skin crisp.

- Tuck a lemon half and onion quarters into the cavity; smash a couple of garlic cloves in there too.

**2. Set the oven**  
- Preheat to 200 °C (180 °C fan) and place a rack in the middle.

**3. Roast the chicken**  
- Place the chicken breast-side up in the roasting tin. Roast for 10 minutes, then turn it so the underside browns.  
- After another 10 minutes, turn it back. You want even colour all around.  
- Keep an eye on it; after 60–75 minutes the thigh should reach 74 °C. If you don’t have a thermometer, check that the juices run clear when you pierce the thickest part.

**4. Prepare the potatoes**  
- While the chicken is on, cube the potatoes into 2 cm pieces.  
- Toss them with olive oil, salt, pepper, and thyme.  
- Spread on a baking sheet and roast alongside the chicken for the last 40 minutes, turning halfway. They’ll go golden and fluffy.

**5. Steam the green beans**  
- Blanch the beans in salted boiling water for 3 minutes, then plunge into cold water to stop the cooking.  
- Toss in a pan with olive oil, smoked paprika, honey, and butter. Heat through for 2 minutes — the honey gives a gentle glaze and the paprika a hint of warmth.

**6. Rest and carve**  
- When the chicken is done, move it to a carving board and cover loosely with foil. Let it rest 10 minutes — the juices redistribute and the meat stays moist.  
- Carve into portions, drizzle with the pan juices, and plate alongside potatoes and beans.

## Roast Chicken for Six
**What you need:**
- 1 whole chicken, 5–6 lb (pick one with good fat on the skin)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder
- 1 tsp smoked paprika
- Salt and pepper, to taste (start with 1½ tsp kosher salt, ¾ tsp pepper)
- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 head garlic, sliced in half horizontally
- ½ cup chicken broth (or water)
- 1 tbsp butter, softened

**Prep:**
1. Preheat the oven to 425 °F (220 °C) so it’s screaming hot before the bird hits the pan.
2. Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead. Cold chicken = rubbery skin.
3. Pat the bird dry inside and out with paper towels—moisture is the enemy of crispy skin.
4. Mix the garlic powder, onion powder, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper. Rub it all over the chicken, then drizzle with olive oil and massage it in.

**Stuff & Truss:**
5. Stuff the cavity with the lemon halves and garlic. This steams the meat from the inside and keeps it juicy.
6. Tie the legs with kitchen twine so the bird cooks evenly and looks tidy.

**Roast:**
7. Place the chicken on a rack in a roasting pan, breast-side up. Pour the broth into the bottom of the pan so the drippings don’t burn.
8. Put it in the oven. Roast for 15 minutes to brown the skin, then reduce the heat to 375 °F (190 °C) and cook for another 35–45 minutes, until the internal temperature at the thickest part of the thigh hits 165 °F (74 °C).
9. Baste once halfway through with the pan juices if you want a darker skin, but don’t fuss too much—open the door too often and you’ll lose heat.

**Rest & Serve:**
10. When done, transfer the chicken to a cutting board, tent it loosely with foil, and let it rest 10–15 minutes. This keeps the juices inside instead of running onto the counter.
11. Carve and serve. Use the pan drippings for a quick gravy if you like: whisk in a tablespoon of flour, add a cup of broth, and simmer until thick.

## Why This Works
- **High heat first** gives the skin a fast sear, locking in flavor.
- **Resting** is non-negotiable; skip it and the meat will be dry.
- **Aromatics in the cavity** steam the meat gently while the outside crisps.

If you want it darker, broil it for the last 2 minutes, but watch it like a hawk—skin goes from golden to burnt in seconds.

Equipment
• Rimmed baking sheet or roasting pan

• Instant-read thermometer

Steps

1. Prep  
   Pat the chicken completely dry with paper towels. Season the cavity with half the salt and pepper. Toss the lemon halves inside; the steam keeps the breast moist.

   Mix the softened butter with lemon juice, garlic, herbs, and remaining salt & pepper. Slide a small amount under the breast skin and the thighs so the meat steams in herb butter as it cooks. Rub the rest on the outside skin.
